extracted.intended_audience: writers, dramatists, literature/theatre students, and psychologists interested in catharsis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for creating or analysing works (especially tragedy) that produce catharsis — covering Aristotle's Poetics, later interpretations (purgation, purification, intellectual clarification), anti-cathartic techniques (Brecht), therapeutic/expressive forms (psychodrama, expressive writing), and social-sharing dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian tragic form and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is “a representation of an action that is heroic and complete and of a certain magnitude—by means of language enriched with all kinds of ornament…: it represents men in action and does not use narrative, and through pity and fear it effects relief [κάθαρσις] to these and similar emotions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft drama as a unified, elevated action (heroic, complete, of magnitude), use enriched language/ornamentation, show characters acting (not mere narration), and aim to arouse pity and fear so the audience experiences cathartic relief. This passage functions as a multipart production rubric (form, style, and emotional path).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for purification/purgation of excessive passions (purgation theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catharsis understood as purgation/purification: “It is the human soul that is purged of its excessive passions.” (F. L. Lucas advocates translating katharsis as purgation.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting this interpretation, design scenes that allow the audience to vicariously experience and be rid of excessive pity/fear (or other passions), returning them to emotional balance. Note scholarly objections (see Else) that caution against treating the audience as patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume therapeutic cure—target normal auditors (Else critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerald F. Else argues against the medical/purgation reading: Aristotle presupposes 'normal' auditors and there is 'not a word to support' the idea that drama's end is to cure pathological states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating tragedy, avoid designing with the explicit assumption that the audience are dysfunctional patients needing cure; instead consider aesthetic/auditory norms and how emotions function in a normal audience's experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis as intellectual clarification/learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'clarification' theory sees catharsis as intellectual pleasure—an outcome of learning and inference (mimesis) that clarifies emotions and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plot and moments of recognition/anagnorisis so the audience gains intellectual insight; catharsis can be achieved via understanding and inference as much as via emotional purge. This aligns with Aristotle's link between mimesis and pleasure in learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lessing's corrective/ethical balancing function
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing interprets catharsis as 'purification' that brings pity and fear into their proper balance: 'Tragedy brings them back to a virtuous and happy mean.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose tragedy to correct extremes of feeling—use plot and characterization to teach an emotional middle ground rather than simply shocking or admonishing the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brechtian anti-catharsis / distancing (Verfremdungseffekt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bertolt Brecht deliberately subverted catharsis: he left significant emotions unresolved and used a distancing effect so the audience would be prompted to take political/social action rather than undergo passive cathartic resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aim is to provoke thought or action instead of relief, design works that prevent complete emotional assimilation/identification (techniques: breaking the fourth wall, episodic structure, alienation devices) so emotions remain unresolved and spur engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of spectator identification (Brecht's view of catharsis as identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brecht identified catharsis with the spectator's identification/complete adhesion to characters and actions, which he viewed as politically and aesthetically counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent passive absorption, limit devices that encourage total empathy or identification (e.g., glamorising characters) and instead foreground critique and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychodrama / expressive enactment techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychodrama uses spontaneous dramatization, role playing, and dramatic self-presentation (often on a stage with props) to reenact real-life situations so participants can evaluate behaviour and gain insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For therapeutic or workshop contexts, use enactment, role-reversal, and reflection phases so individuals experience, express, and cognitively process emotions; these practices are designed to produce cathartic insight and behavioral change (origin: Jacob Moreno).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primal therapy: re-experiencing and full expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Primal therapy elicits sequential re-experiencing of childhood pain and full expression of resulting pain (capitalized as 'Pain') so the neurosis-causative repressed pain is processed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or representing primal-like techniques, emphasize safe, guided re-experiencing and full affective expression as means to emotional resolution; note Janov's critique of purely 'talking therapies.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sharing as collective catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernard Rimé's research: individuals share emotional episodes (80–95% of cases); sharing prompts secondary/tertiary social sharing and can produce social integration, strengthening of beliefs, renewed trust, and self-confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create narratives or interventions that facilitate social communication about emotional experiences (e.g., scenes that invite discussion, communal rituals) if the goal is collective processing; be aware of dynamics of repeated reactivation and 'emotional overheating.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives for sharing positive vs negative events (capitalization vs venting/support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies show people share positive events to 'capitalize' (augment positive affect, inform, gain attention) and negative events to vent, understand, bond, and gain social support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing stories or group exercises, tailor prompts: use celebratory/shared recall to boost positive affects, and provide supportive framing for negative-event sharing to foster understanding and support rather than rumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive writing as a mechanism (mixed evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressive writing (written disclosure of thoughts and feelings) has been reported (Frattaroli meta-analysis) to enhance mental health, but other studies show it can impede recovery in some contexts (e.g., marital separation) and effects are mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expressive-writing prompts cautiously: they can facilitate catharsis and insight but may also exacerbate distress depending on timing/context; monitor outcomes and avoid one-size-fits-all prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical cautions and potential harms of cathartic interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research cautions that 'blowing off steam' may reduce short-term physiological stress but can reinforce aggressive behaviour; group debriefing and other cathartic interventions have shown negative effects in some meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying cathartic techniques (in drama therapy, interventions, or narrative design claiming therapeutic effects), balance intended benefits against risks documented in empirical studies — pilot, provide support, and avoid practices shown to impede recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective response stages to large emotional events (Pennebaker & Harber)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-stage model after collective emotional events: 'emergency' (first month: abundant thoughts/talk/media), 'plateau' (second month: reduced integration), and 'extinction' (after second month: return to normalcy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers/scholars addressing communal trauma, consider narrative timing and pacing to align with communal processing phases; interventions or storytelling may play different roles across these stages.
